title: Threats, restricting the risks, and protecting the data

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The threats to data security posed by networks and the internet; methods that restrict the risks; and security methods designed to protect the data itself.

blocks.heading: The threats
blocks.text: Connecting to a network connects the network to you, and four threats arrive with it. Malware is software written to harm: a virus spreads from file to file and machine to machine, damaging what it touches, and spyware sits quietly recording the user's activity - keys typed, sites visited - and sends it to whoever planted it. Hackers probe for openings: unauthorised users who gain access through weak passwords and unprotected services, reading or changing what they should never have reached. Phishing is a message that tricks the user into visiting a fake site or revealing details: the email that claims to be the bank, the link that leads to a page built to look like the bank's. Pharming does without the user's cooperation: the user is redirected to a fake site though they typed the right address, for example after the domain's address record has been altered, so the trap is on the road, not in the message. The two are told apart by the user's part in it: phishing needs a click or a reply, whereas pharming works without any action of the user's - the test is to ask what the user did. Spyware rides in on both roads - arriving hidden in downloads, arriving hidden in phishing attachments - and sits between the two camps: like a virus it arrives as software, like a keylogger it acts in silence, so it is found by anti-spyware scans and starved by the same caution that starves the phisher.

blocks.heading: Restricting the risks
blocks.text: Risks cannot all be removed, and restricting them means shrinking what each threat can reach. Access rights shrink what an intruder or an error finds: each user gets only what their work needs, so a stolen till password reaches prices, not payrolls. User training shrinks the human opening: staff told that the bank never asks for details by email, and told to take such requests to a manager, starve the phisher, because the trick works on the unprepared. Firewalls shrink the network opening: unsolicited connections from outside stop at the edge, so probes and unwanted traffic end at the wall rather than at the records. Copies beyond the one site shrink the loss: a second copy at another place means a fire, a theft or a locked-away ransom at the office loses a day at most, because the data survives beyond the building. And keeping software updated shrinks the openings that come with time: an unpatched system is a door whose lock has been published, so the updates are the shutting of it. A budget answer for any named threat is drawn from this list in two moves: name the route the threat takes, then name the measure that owns that route, because risk restriction is the pairing of the two, not a list of everything known.

blocks.heading: Protecting the data itself
blocks.text: Two methods protect the data rather than the routes to it. Encryption makes the data meaningless without the key: each file is scrambled by a method that needs its key to undo, so a stolen laptop holds scrambled bytes, a copied transmission carries scrambled bytes, and whoever took them has nothing readable. Encryption's limits are as important as its power: the data can still be intercepted - the thief still takes the file - and encryption says nothing about who sent the data, so a message can be unreadable to strangers and still come from an impostor. Proving authorship is the digital signature's job, met in the last unit. Access rights are the second method, and they work after the gate is opened: rights decide which users may read, change or delete each file or record, so the clerk reads the prices but cannot change them, and the partner's case files stay with the partners. Together the two answer the two fears: taken data that cannot be read, and authorised users who cannot reach past their work. The pairing also names each method’s blind spot: encryption without access rights leaves the authorised careless reader free, and access rights without encryption leave the taken file open, so a serious arrangement uses both, each covering the other’s gap.

blocks.heading: Common errors
blocks.text: Two slips recur. Phishing and pharming described as each other: phishing needs a click or a reply, pharming redirects without the user's action - the test is to ask whether the user acted on a message or typed the right address and was redirected anyway. And encryption given the powers of a guard and a witness: encrypted data can still be intercepted, and encryption does not prove who sent it - the test is whether the data can still be taken, which it can, so encryption protects meaning, not access or authorship.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The integrity that checking protects is 6.2's whole subject, and the ethics of holding and using people's data is 7.1's. The encrypted files travel the networks of 2.1, and their safety in storage leans on the devices of 3.1.
